# On the Peculiar Comfort of Autumn

There's something about October that makes me want to sit still. Not lazily, but purposefully—the way you'd settle into a good book knowing you have nowhere else to be.

The world is actively dying right now. Trees are releasing their leaves in a spectacular surrender, and instead of this being sad, we've collectively decided it's beautiful. Maybe that's the real genius of autumn: it rebrands endings as aesthetics. We don't mourn the year's death; we photograph it in golden hour.

I think humans need this permission. We spend so much energy fighting entropy—organizing closets, making resolutions, believing in permanence. Autumn whispers that letting go isn't failure. The tree doesn't apologize for dropping its leaves. It just does what its nature requires.

There's also something democratizing about it. Everyone's autumn is the same season. Rich or poor, famous or anonymous, we all get the same shortened days, the same cooling air, the same soft light that makes everything look forgivable. For a moment, we're all subject to the same natural timeline that doesn't care about our productivity or our plans.

And that's oddly freeing.

I think I love autumn because it's honest in a way the rest of the year isn't. Spring promises renewal. Summer promises forever. Winter promises rest but it's often brutal. But autumn? Autumn just says: *this is happening, and it's okay*. Everything beautiful is temporary. Everything ending was also a beginning. Watch closely. This won't last.
